sections.minutes: sum of the subsection time boxes (54)
sections.order_note: Teaching order follows one request: the client finds a node in a zone (1), the node reaches private targets through security groups (2), the type decides which layer is read (3), listener rules choose a target group (4), the HTTPS listener decrypts (5) and the request may be encrypted again or passed through (6), the algorithm or a sticky cookie picks the target (7), health checks decide who is eligible and how a target leaves (8), cross-zone spreads requests over zones (9); then the two other types follow their own request: the Network Load Balancer (10) and the Gateway Load Balancer (11); and the bill (12). sections.heading: A load balancer gives each enabled Availability Zone its own node

plan.problem: A web application runs on one instance in one Availability Zone. If the instance or its zone fails, every user sees an error, and nobody can fix it fast enough by hand.
trace: **Enable zones.** You give an Application Load Balancer [at least two Availability Zone subnets], each [from a different Availability Zone] (elb-alb-subnets-two-azs-different); Elastic Load Balancing [creates a load balancer node] [in the Availability Zone] for each one (elb-node-per-enabled-az).

**Resolve the name.** The client looks up the load balancer's DNS name. [The DNS entry is controlled by Amazon] and returns the [IP addresses of the load balancer nodes] (elb-dns-returns-node-ips): an ALB has [one IP address per enabled Availability Zone] (elb-alb-one-ip-per-enabled-az).

**Scale.** As traffic changes, Elastic Load Balancing [scales your load balancer] and updates the DNS entry, which has a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds] so that the [IP addresses can be remapped quickly] (elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap).
**Forward.** The node that receives the request [selects a healthy registered target] and sends the request [using its private IP address] (elb-node-sends-to-target-private-ip).
plan.table: What survives what (columns: Design | An instance fails | An Availability Zone fails): one instance with an Elastic IP address | down until someone moves the address; AWS describes [rapidly remapping the address to another instance] (ec2-eip-mask-instance-failure-remap) | down; load balancer, all targets in one zone | the other targets serve | down: [Your production workload exists only in a single Availability Zone] is an anti-pattern (vpc-wa-rel10-bp01-avoid-single-points-of-failure); load balancer, targets in two or more zones | the other targets serve | targets in the other zones serve (elb-wa-rel10-load-balancers-in-front-of-compute).
plan.why: Why a node in every zone? The loss of one zone then removes one entry point, not all of them; AWS asks you to [avoid single points of failure, including the underlying physical infrastructure] (vpc-wa-rel10-bp01-avoid-single-points-of-failure).
plan.exam_signal: "remove the single point of failure of a web tier that runs on one instance" points to a load balancer with targets in two or more Availability Zones: [Place traffic directors such as load balancers] [in front of your compute resources] (elb-wa-rel10-load-balancers-in-front-of-compute); "use a friendly domain name" points to a Route 53 alias record: [create an alias record] (elb-custom-domain-route53-alias), never the node addresses.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: subnet size, empty subnets and more than one Region. Each ALB subnet needs [at least a `/27` bitmask] and [at least eight free IP addresses] (elb-alb-subnet-min-27-eight-free-ips). [Avoid creating empty subnets]: the ALB still publishes their zonal addresses, which [triggers 503 errors for HTTP requests] (elb-alb-empty-subnet-503). A Network Load Balancer can start in one zone: [select at least one Availability Zone] (elb-nlb-at-least-one-az). A load balancer serves the zones you enable; to spread traffic over [load balancers in one or more AWS Regions], put [AWS Global Accelerator] in front (elb-ga-alb-multiple-regions; chapter 15). At most 90 words. Do not call a load balancer 'Regional': no verified fact says it (brief.v0 d088).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a load balancer gives each zone its own entry point and sends each request to a healthy target. The thing to watch is that clients must use its DNS name, not its IP addresses.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team registers web instances in AZ 1, AZ 2 and AZ 3, but enables only AZ 1 and AZ 2 on the Application Load Balancer. Do the instances in AZ 3 receive requests? Answer: no; for targets in a zone that is not enabled, [these registered targets do not receive traffic] (elb-targets-in-disabled-az-no-traffic). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: Targets can stay private and accept traffic only from the load balancer

plan.problem: The web servers must answer users on the internet, but nobody may reach a server directly, around the load balancer and its rules.
trace: **Choose the scheme.** At creation you pick an [internal load balancer or an internet-facing load balancer] (elb-scheme-choose-internal-or-internet-facing). Internet-facing nodes [have public IP addresses] (elb-internet-facing-nodes-public-ips); internal nodes [have only private IP addresses] and serve [clients with access to the VPC] (elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only).

**Reach the target privately.** Both schemes route to targets [using private IP addresses], so the targets [do not need public IP addresses] (elb-targets-need-no-public-ip): put them in private subnets.

**Filter at the load balancer.** The ALB security group controls the [traffic that is allowed to reach and leave] (elb-alb-security-group-controls-traffic); its rules must [allow traffic in both directions] on [both the listener and the health check ports] (elb-alb-sg-listener-and-health-check-ports).

**Filter at the target.** The targets' security group names [the load balancer's security group as the source], so the targets [receive traffic exclusively from the load balancer] (elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg).
plan.table: Security groups by type (columns: Type | Security groups | Note): Application Load Balancer | yes: [Security Groups] (elb-compare-security-groups-not-gwlb) | the console preselects the VPC default group: [We preselect the default security group] (elb-alb-default-sg-preselected); Network Load Balancer | only if you add them [when you create it] (elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation) | without one, [all client traffic can reach] the listeners (elb-nlb-no-sg-all-traffic-allowed); Gateway Load Balancer | none: they [do not have associated security groups] (elb-gwlb-no-security-groups) | the appliances' rules [must use IP addresses to allow traffic].
plan.why: Why name a security group instead of addresses? The nodes' addresses change as the load balancer scales ([IP addresses can be remapped quickly], elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap); a rule that names the load balancer's group keeps working.
plan.exam_signal: "the instances must accept traffic only from the load balancer" points to a target security group rule whose source is the load balancer's security group (elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg; chapter 10 shows the same chain: [Allows inbound HTTPS access from the load balancer], vpc-sg-chain-web-allows-lb-sg); "a web tier and a private application tier" points to an internet-facing load balancer for the web servers and an internal one for the application servers: [both internal and internet-facing load balancers] (elb-multi-tier-internet-facing-plus-internal).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: a network ACL on the target subnets must allow the return traffic on [ports 1024-65535] (vpc-nacl-ephemeral-natgw-elb-lambda-1024-65535); a deny for all traffic there means [your load balancer can't carry out health checks on the instances] (vpc-nacl-elb-health-check-deny). Chapter 10 owns network ACLs: an xref, no detail.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: put the targets in private subnets and let their security group accept only the load balancer's group. The thing to watch is the health check port, which the rules must allow too.
plan.stop_and_answer: An internet-facing ALB works. A developer replaces the target rule that names the load balancer's security group with a rule that allows port 80 from the whole VPC range. Do requests through the load balancer still work, and what changed? Answer: they still work, because the targets see the load balancer's private address as the source: server logs [only contain the IP address] of the load balancer (elb-alb-xff-holds-client-ip); but now every resource in the VPC can reach the targets directly.

sections.heading: Each load balancer type reads a different layer of the traffic
sections.diagram: elb-type-ladder, after the table (its alt and caption count toward this subsection: keep the alt at about 45 words)

plan.problem: A customer asks for 'a load balancer'. AWS has three current types, and the wrong one cannot do what the application needs.
trace: **Layer 7: read the request.** An Application Load Balancer [functions at the application layer] (elb-alb-layer-7), so it can route on fields such as [host-header] and [path-pattern] (elb-alb-condition-types).

**Layer 4: read the connection.** A Network Load Balancer works at the [fourth layer of the Open Systems Interconnection] model and handles [millions of requests per second] (elb-nlb-millions-of-requests-per-second); it picks a target [using a flow hash algorithm] (elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection).
**Layer 3: read the packet.** A Gateway Load Balancer [operates at the third layer] and [listens for all IP packets across all ports] (elb-gwlb-layer-3-all-ports).
plan.table: Features by type (columns: Feature | ALB | NLB | GWLB): security groups | yes | yes | no ([Security Groups], elb-compare-security-groups-not-gwlb); static or Elastic IP address | no | yes | no ([IP address - Static, Elastic], elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only); Lambda function targets | yes | no | no ([do not support the `lambda` target type], elb-lambda-target-alb-only); user authentication | yes | no | no ([User Authentication], elb-compare-user-authentication-alb-only); AWS WAF | yes ([Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer], waf-protected-resource-types) | not in the list | not in the list. Write the NLB and GWLB WAF cells as 'not in the list of protected resources'; no fact says 'cannot'. This table must not repeat the fast type table (layer, protocols, targets).
plan.why: Why can a Network Load Balancer not route by path? It reads connections, not requests: for a layer 7 protocol [no special handling exists in Network Load Balancer] because the [Network Load Balancer is operating at layer 4] (elb-nlb-faq-websockets-tcp-no-special-handling).
plan.exam_signal: "route requests by URL path or host name" points to an Application Load Balancer ([If you need to load balance HTTP requests], elb-choose-alb-for-http-flexible-management); "static IP addresses", "TCP or UDP" or "extreme performance" point to a Network Load Balancer ([extreme performance and static IP is needed], elb-choose-nlb-for-layer4-extreme-performance-static-ip); "third-party firewall appliances" points to a Gateway Load Balancer ([third-party virtual appliances], elb-choose-gwlb-for-third-party-appliances).
plan.body_extras: One sentence on the old type: the Classic Load Balancer is the [previous generation of load balancers], and AWS recommends to [migrate to a current generation load balancer] (elb-classic-previous-generation-migrate); [you cannot convert one load balancer type] into another (elb-faq-cannot-convert-load-balancer-type). The Classic Load Balancer is never a correct answer in this chapter.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: HTTP routing means an Application Load Balancer, fixed addresses or raw TCP and UDP mean a Network Load Balancer, and appliances mean a Gateway Load Balancer. The thing to watch is that a Network Load Balancer never reads the URL.
plan.stop_and_answer: A multiplayer game uses UDP on one port and needs the lowest latency. A teammate proposes an Application Load Balancer because it has more features. Which type fits? Answer: a Network Load Balancer; ALB listeners take only [HTTP, HTTPS] (elb-alb-listener-protocols-http-https), while NLB listeners take [TCP, TLS, UDP] (elb-nlb-listener-protocols).

sections.heading: Listener rules are checked in priority order, and the default rule comes last

plan.problem: A company runs five services under two domain names. One load balancer for each service multiplies the hourly charges and the certificates to manage.
trace: **Listen.** A listener is [a process that checks for connection requests], [configured with a protocol and port number] (elb-listener-checks-connection-requests); without one, an ALB [can't receive traffic from clients] (elb-alb-needs-listener-to-receive-traffic).

**Check rules in order.** The ALB [Evaluates the listener rules in priority order] (elb-alb-rules-priority-then-algorithm), [from the lowest value to the highest value]; [The default rule is evaluated last] (elb-alb-rules-lowest-priority-first). A priority is a value from [1 to 50,000] (elb-alb-rule-priority-1-to-50000).

**Match conditions.** A rule can match on [host-header], [path-pattern], [query-string] or [source-ip] (elb-alb-condition-types), so one ALB can [route requests to multiple domains] [using a single load balancer] (elb-alb-host-conditions-many-domains-one-lb).

**Act.** Each rule has [exactly one of the following actions]: [`forward`, `redirect`, or `fixed-response`] (elb-alb-rule-one-routing-action-last); a redirect sends [HTTP to HTTPS] as a [permanent (HTTP 301)] redirect (elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https).
plan.table: One ALB, several services (columns: Priority | Condition | Action): 10 | host is api.example.com | forward to target group api; 20 | path is /reports/* | forward to target group reports; 30 | path is /old/* | redirect to /new/; default | none | forward to target group web. Example rows, no fact needed except where a cell states an AWS rule. Mention under the table that the HTTP listener on port 80 holds one redirect rule to HTTPS (elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb).
plan.why: Why one load balancer for many services? Each load balancer is billed for [each hour or partial hour] (elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour), and an ALB's rule evaluations cost nothing for the [first 10 processed rules are free] (elb-alb-lcu-first-10-rules-free). No AWS sentence says 'one ALB is cheaper than many': derive it from these two facts, do not quote it as AWS's claim (brief.v0 d103).
plan.exam_signal: "route /api to one service and /images to another" or "several domain names on one endpoint" points to ALB listener rules with path or host conditions: [forward requests based on the URL] (elb-alb-path-conditions-smaller-services); "send HTTP users to HTTPS" points to a redirect action on the HTTP listener (elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https).
plan.try_it: Try it callout for elb-t02 after the table, ending with its task comment.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: weights, rewrites and limits. A forward action can split traffic when you [specify a weight for each target group] (elb-alb-weighted-forward-traffic-split), each from [0 to 999] (elb-weighted-target-group-weight-0-to-999); if one group is empty or unhealthy, the load balancer [does not automatically fail over] (elb-alb-weighted-no-auto-failover). A transform [rewrites inbound requests before they are routed] and [does not change the routing decision] (elb-alb-transforms-rewrite-host-url). An ALB has [100 rules] by default (elb-alb-quota-rules-per-lb), and one action can use [5 target groups] (elb-alb-quota-target-groups-per-action). At most 90 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: one Application Load Balancer can serve many services with host and path rules. The thing to watch is rule priority, because the lowest number is checked first.
plan.stop_and_answer: The HTTPS listener has only its default rule, which forwards to target group web. The team wants requests for /admin to go to target group admin. Can they add a path condition to the default rule? Answer: no; [The default rule can't have conditions] (elb-alb-default-rule-last-no-conditions); add a new rule with a priority. Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: An HTTPS listener decrypts requests at the load balancer with its certificate

plan.problem: Browsers must reach the site over HTTPS on several domain names. A certificate on every instance means installing and renewing it on every instance.
trace: **Deploy a certificate.** An HTTPS listener uses a certificate to [terminate the front-end connection] and decrypt requests (elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts); you [must specify exactly one certificate], the default certificate (acm-alb-https-listener-default-certificate), and ACM can [deploy ACM certificates on the load balancer] (acm-elb-deploys-on-load-balancer).

**Negotiate.** A security policy is [a combination of protocols and ciphers] used to [negotiate SSL connections] (elb-alb-security-policy-protocols-ciphers); [An HTTPS listener requires a security policy] (elb-alb-https-default-security-policy).

**Pick the certificate by name.** With a certificate list the listener can [support multiple domains on the same port] and [provide a different certificate for each domain], chosen by a [smart certificate selection algorithm with support for SNI] (elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).

**Forward.** The load balancer sends the decrypted request on; the X-Forwarded-Proto header lets the target [identify the protocol (HTTP or HTTPS)] the client used (elb-alb-xff-proto-original-protocol).
plan.table: Where the certificate comes from (columns: Source | Renewal | Note): issued by ACM | [can be renewed automatically] (elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically) | renewal [does not affect in-flight requests] (acm-alb-renewal-in-flight); imported into ACM from another certificate authority | ACM [does not manage the renewal process] (acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) | [you must monitor the expiration date] (elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically); uploaded to IAM | you renew it | you can [upload the certificate] to IAM instead of ACM (acm-alb-certificate-from-acm-or-iam). Do not put the Region rule in this table: the Spot the bug uses it.
plan.why: Why end TLS at the load balancer? Elastic Load Balancing [performs the work of encrypting and decrypting] instead of each instance (elb-offload-encryption-to-lb), and one managed certificate replaces one per instance.
plan.exam_signal: "offload TLS from the web servers" or "certificates that renew automatically" points to an HTTPS listener with an ACM certificate (elb-offload-encryption-to-lb, elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically); "several domain names on one HTTPS listener" points to a certificate list with SNI (elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: without a policy the console uses [ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-PQ-2025-09], while the AWS CLI and CloudFormation use [ELBSecurityPolicy-2016-08] (elb-alb-https-default-security-policy); AWS asks you to choose [the strongest cipher suites supported by the clients] (acm-wa-alb-strongest-security-policy).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug (one of the two in the file): an ALB runs in US West (Oregon). The team requests its ACM certificate in US East (N. Virginia), as it did for CloudFront, and cannot select it on the HTTPS listener. Reveal: ACM certificates [must be in the same Region] as the resource that uses them; [The only exception is Amazon CloudFront] (acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource). Request the certificate in US West (Oregon). Place it after the Exam trap and before Say it; about 65 words with its reveal.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the load balancer holds the certificate and does the TLS work, so the instances do not. The thing to watch is that the load balancer then sees the decrypted request.
plan.stop_and_answer: One HTTPS listener has certificates for shop.example.com and help.example.com. The team adds a third domain, news.example.org. Does it need a new listener or a new load balancer? Answer: no; add the certificate to the listener's certificate list; an ALB holds [25] certificates by default besides the default certificate (acm-alb-certificates-per-load-balancer). A wildcard certificate would not cover a different parent domain.

sections.heading: Encryption to the targets needs a second TLS connection or a pass-through
sections.diagram: elb-tls-paths, after the trace (its alt and caption count toward this subsection: keep the alt at about 45 words)

plan.problem: An auditor requires that patient data stay encrypted in transit all the way to the servers. The HTTPS listener alone ends the encryption at the load balancer.
trace: **Terminate.** The HTTPS listener ends TLS at the load balancer (previous subsection). With an HTTP target group, the hop from the load balancer to the target is plain HTTP.

**Re-encrypt.** With an HTTPS target group, the ALB opens a second TLS connection to each target. It encrypts that hop, but [only encryption is supported to the back-ends] (elb-alb-faq-no-backend-server-authentication).

**Pass through.** If the targets themselves must decrypt, use [a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443], which [passes encrypted traffic through to the targets] (elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp).

**Or terminate on the NLB.** A TLS listener on a Network Load Balancer also ends TLS and needs you to [deploy at least one SSL server certificate] (elb-nlb-tls-listener-terminate-tcp-passthrough); the [Source IP continues to be preserved] [even if you terminate TLS] (elb-nlb-faq-source-ip-preserved-with-tls).
plan.table: Three paths (columns: Path | Load balancer sees the request | Last hop encrypted | Path rules possible): ALB HTTPS listener + HTTP target group | yes | no | yes; ALB HTTPS listener + HTTPS target group | yes | yes | yes; NLB TCP listener on port 443 | no: it [passes encrypted traffic through to the targets] (elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp) | yes | no (layer 4). Keep this table; the fast file has no TLS table.
plan.why: Why decrypt in the middle at all? Layer 7 features need the plain request: path rules, headers and user sign-in all read it, so an ALB must decrypt before it can route (elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts).
plan.exam_signal: "encrypt data in transit end to end" together with HTTP routing points to an HTTPS listener plus an HTTPS target group; "the load balancer must not decrypt the traffic" or "the instances hold the certificates" points to a Network Load Balancer TCP listener on port 443 (elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: mutual TLS and sign-in at the listener. With mutual TLS, passthrough mode [sends the entire client certificate chain] to the target [without verifying it], and verify mode [performs X.509 client certificate authentication] (elb-alb-mtls-passthrough-vs-verify) with a trust store: [Create a new trust store resource], then [Attach the trust store to the listener] (elb-alb-mtls-verify-trust-store). An ALB can also sign users in through an [OpenID Connect (OIDC) compliant] provider or Amazon Cognito (elb-alb-user-authentication-idps); these actions are [supported only with HTTPS listeners] (cognito-alb-authenticate-cognito-https-only). For service-to-service calls it can [verify JSON Web Tokens (JWT)] (elb-alb-jwt-verification-m2m). At most 90 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: for encryption all the way, re-encrypt to HTTPS targets or pass TLS through a Network Load Balancer. The thing to watch is that the Application Load Balancer does not check the target's certificate.
plan.stop_and_answer: Targets behind an ALB listen on port 443 with a self-signed certificate, and the target group protocol is HTTPS. Does the load balancer refuse to connect? Answer: no; [The load balancer does not validate these certificates], so [self-signed certificates or certificates that have expired] work (elb-alb-target-https-no-cert-validation). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: Sticky sessions send a user back to one target and bypass the algorithm

plan.problem: An application keeps each user's session in the memory of the instance that served the first request. When the next request lands on another instance, the user is signed out.
trace: **First request.** The target group's routing algorithm picks the target: [round robin] by default, or [least outstanding requests] or [weighted random] (elb-alb-routing-algorithms-three).

**Set the cookie.** Stickiness is [enabled at the target group level] with [duration-based cookies and application-based cookies] (elb-alb-sticky-duration-vs-application-cookie); the duration-based cookie is the [load balancer generated cookie] [`AWSALB`] (elb-alb-duration-cookie-awsalb).

**Later requests.** The algorithm was [used for the initial target selection]; later requests from the same client go to the same target, [bypassing the selected routing algorithm] (elb-alb-sticky-bypasses-algorithm).
**Expire.** A duration-based cookie lasts [1 day] by default and can be set from [1 second] to [7 days] (elb-alb-lb-cookie-duration-default-1-day).
plan.table: Which routing algorithm (columns: Algorithm | Fits | Note): round robin | requests [similar in complexity] (elb-alb-round-robin-use) | the default; least outstanding requests | requests that [vary in complexity] (elb-alb-least-outstanding-requests-use) | sends to the [lowest number of in progress requests]; weighted random | [Automatic Target Weights (ATW) anomaly mitigation] | [can not be used with slow start mode] (elb-alb-weighted-random-no-sticky-slow-start). Keep the sticky-sessions limit of weighted random for the Stop and answer.
plan.why: Why not stop at stickiness? It can cause an [uneven distribution of connections and flows] (elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat), and the session still lives on one instance; AWS calls a [centralized session management data store] the ideal answer [when your fleet of web servers is elastic] (elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers).
plan.exam_signal: "the application stores session state on the web server, and the code cannot change" points to sticky sessions ([servers that maintain state information], elb-alb-sticky-for-stateful-servers); "the web tier must be stateless" or "sessions must survive the loss of an instance" points to a session store in a [database, cache, or external files] (ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data; chapter 29).
plan.startup_example: Startup example callout (at most 60 words with its label, story only, no AWS rule): Callvale keeps user sessions in the memory of each web instance. For the launch, the team turns on duration-based stickiness on the target group, so that each user returns to the same instance. Callvale accepts this until chapter 29 moves the sessions to a cache.
plan.body_extras: One sentence on the Network Load Balancer: its stickiness type is source IP ([The possible value is `source_ip`], elb-nlb-sticky-source-ip), so [all clients behind the same NAT device] reach one target (elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: sticky sessions send a user back to the same instance with a cookie. The thing to watch is that the session still lives on that one instance, so move it to a shared store.
plan.stop_and_answer: A target group uses weighted random routing with anomaly mitigation. The team now also needs sticky sessions. Can it keep the algorithm? Answer: no; weighted random [can not be used with sticky sessions] (elb-alb-weighted-random-no-sticky-slow-start); switch to round robin or least outstanding requests.

sections.heading: Health checks decide which registered targets receive requests
sections.diagram: elb-target-states, after the trace (its alt and caption count toward this subsection: keep the alt at about 40 words)

plan.problem: An instance can be running but broken: its web server hangs. The load balancer must notice, and stop sending users to it.
trace: **Register.** A new target is [`initial`] while the load balancer is [performing the initial health checks on the target] (elb-alb-target-state-initial).

**Check.** Settings live [on a per target group basis] (elb-health-checks-per-target-group): an ALB sends an HTTP request to the path [The default is /.] (elb-alb-health-check-path-default-slash) and expects [The default value is 200] (elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200).

**Fail and recover.** After [2 consecutive failed health checks] the target is unhealthy (elb-alb-unhealthy-threshold-default-2), and [it stops routing traffic to that target]; when the target passes again, it [resumes routing traffic to that target] (elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume).

**Leave.** On deregistration the load balancer [stops routing requests to a target], which [enters the `draining` state] [until in-flight requests have completed] (elb-deregister-stops-routing-draining), for at most the deregistration delay of [300 seconds] by default (elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds); then its state is [`unused`] (elb-alb-deregistration-draining-then-unused).
plan.table: Health check defaults (columns: Setting | ALB | NLB): protocol | [The default is the HTTP protocol] (elb-alb-health-check-protocol-default-http) | [The default is the TCP protocol] (elb-nlb-health-check-protocol-default-tcp); interval | [30 seconds] (elb-alb-health-check-interval-default-30-seconds) | [30 seconds] (elb-nlb-health-check-interval-default-30-seconds); unhealthy after | [2 consecutive failed health checks] (elb-alb-unhealthy-threshold-default-2) | [2 consecutive failed health checks] (elb-nlb-unhealthy-threshold-default-2); success codes | [The default value is 200] | [200-399] (elb-nlb-health-check-success-codes-default-200-399). Do not repeat in the table what the trace already linked; drop the success code row if the subsection runs over.
plan.why: Why does the load balancer not replace the instance? It routes; EC2 Auto Scaling replaces. With ELB health checks on the group, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it] and [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance] (ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace); by default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing] checks (ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default). Chapter 17 owns the group: an xref.
plan.exam_signal: "instances keep running but stop responding, and they must be replaced automatically" points to the ELB health check type on the Auto Scaling group: [select an ELB health check] (ec2-auto-scaling-faq-which-health-check-type); "requests fail while instances are removed during scale-in" points to the deregistration delay, which helps [in-flight requests to the target to complete] (elb-alb-deregistration-waits-for-in-flight).
plan.try_it: Try it callout for elb-t03 after the table, ending with its task comment.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: reading 502, 503 and 504. A 503 can mean that the target groups [have no registered targets] (elb-alb-503-no-registered-targets). A 504 can mean a target that did not answer [before the idle timeout period elapsed] (elb-alb-504-target-no-response-idle-timeout), which is [60 seconds] by default (elb-alb-idle-timeout-default-60-seconds), or a network ACL that blocks [ephemeral ports (1024-65535)] (elb-alb-504-nacl-ephemeral-ports). A 502 can mean the load balancer [received a TCP RST from the target] (elb-alb-502-bad-target-response). [HTTPCode\_ELB\_5XX\_Count] counts errors that [originate from the load balancer] (elb-alb-metric-httpcode-elb-5xx). At most 90 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: health checks decide who gets requests, and a failing target stops getting them. The thing to watch is that the load balancer does not replace it; EC2 Auto Scaling does.
plan.stop_and_answer: A new target passes its first health check right after registration, and the healthy threshold is 5. Does it receive requests now, or after five passes? Answer: now; routing starts when it [passes the first initial health check], [irrespective of the configured threshold] (elb-new-target-after-first-health-check).

sections.heading: Cross-zone load balancing spreads requests over the targets in every enabled zone

plan.problem: Zone 1 has two targets and zone 2 has six. Requests should be shared by target, not by zone, or the two targets in zone 1 overload.
trace: **Clients spread over nodes.** DNS returns the node addresses of all enabled zones (elb-dns-returns-node-ips, previous subsections), so each node receives a share of the clients.
**Cross-zone on.** Each node distributes traffic across the [registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones] (elb-cross-zone-what-it-does).
**Cross-zone off.** Each node uses only the [registered targets in its Availability Zone] (elb-cross-zone-what-it-does), so a zone with fewer targets gives each of them more requests.
plan.table: Cross-zone by type (columns: Type | Default | Data transfer between zones): Application Load Balancer | [on by default]; it [cannot be changed at the load balancer level] but is [possible at the target group level] (elb-alb-cross-zone-on-by-default) | [you are not charged] (elb-alb-cross-zone-no-data-transfer-charge); Network Load Balancer | off: [cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default] (elb-nlb-gwlb-cross-zone-off-by-default) | [charged for regional data transfer between Availability Zones] (elb-nlb-faq-cross-zone-regional-data-transfer-charged); Gateway Load Balancer | off (same fact) | [charged for data transfer between Availability Zones] (elb-gwlb-faq-cross-zone-data-transfer-charged).
plan.why: Why can turning it off make sense? Each zone then serves only its own traffic, and a Network Load Balancer offers [provides stable IP support and zonal isolation] (elb-nlb-faq-key-features). The cost of that choice: with cross-zone on, ALB and NLB [reroute traffic towards targets in healthy Availability Zones] (elb-wa-rel10-cross-zone-reroute-impaired-az).
plan.exam_signal: "uneven load because the Availability Zones hold different numbers of instances" points to cross-zone load balancing (elb-cross-zone-what-it-does); on a Network Load Balancer it adds a charge for data that crosses zones (elb-nlb-faq-cross-zone-regional-data-transfer-charged).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug (the second in the file): a Network Load Balancer with default settings has two targets in AZ 1 and six in AZ 2. Clients spread evenly over both node addresses, and the two AZ 1 targets run much hotter than the others. Reveal: on a Network Load Balancer, [cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default] (elb-nlb-gwlb-cross-zone-off-by-default), so each node uses only its own zone's targets; turn it [on or off at the target group level] or for the load balancer (elb-nlb-cross-zone-lb-and-tg-level), or balance the targets across zones. Place it after the Exam trap and before Say it; about 65 words with its reveal.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: when a whole zone fails. A Network Load Balancer removes the IP address of a zone with no healthy target: the address of the [corresponding subnet from DNS] (elb-nlb-unhealthy-az-removed-from-dns-fail-open). An ALB target group can mark a zone [as unhealthy in DNS] when too few targets are healthy (elb-target-group-health-dns-failover), but client caches keep old answers for up to [60 seconds] (elb-dns-failover-client-cache-60-seconds). A zonal shift moves traffic [away from an impaired Availability Zone] [with a single action] (elb-zonal-shift-what); [Zonal shift is disabled by default] (elb-alb-zonal-shift-off-by-default-one-az). With zonal autoshift, [you authorize AWS to shift away resource traffic] (elb-zonal-autoshift-aws-shifts). At most 90 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: cross-zone load balancing lets every node use every healthy target in every enabled zone. The thing to watch is the default: on and free for an Application Load Balancer, off and charged for a Network Load Balancer.
plan.stop_and_answer: An ALB target group for a reporting service has cross-zone load balancing turned off. The team wants to register a Lambda function in that target group. Does it work? Answer: no; with cross-zone off, [Lambda functions as targets are not supported] (elb-alb-cross-zone-off-no-sticky-no-lambda).

sections.heading: A Network Load Balancer gives static IP addresses and can keep client IPs

plan.problem: A bank's firewall team allows outbound traffic only to fixed IP addresses, and the service must log each caller's IP address for audits.
trace: **One address per zone.** Elastic Load Balancing creates a network interface in each enabled zone and [uses it to get a static IP address]; you can [optionally associate one Elastic IP address] [when you create the Network Load Balancer] (elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip). For an internal one you can [enter a private IPv4 address] (elb-nlb-internal-choose-private-ip).

**Keep the flow.** A node sends each TCP connection to a [single target for the life of the connection] (elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection); for UDP it [maintains UDP flow state based on 5-tuple hash] (elb-nlb-faq-udp-flow-5-tuple-idle).

**Show the client.** A Network Load Balancer [can preserve the source IP addresses of clients]; with preservation off, targets see the [private IP address of the Network Load Balancer] (elb-nlb-client-ip-disabled-source-is-nlb). Proxy protocol version 2 can [send additional connection information] (elb-nlb-proxy-protocol-v2).

**Hand HTTP to an ALB.** For path rules behind fixed addresses, register an ALB as the target; the ALB [takes over the load balancing decision] (elb-nlb-alb-target-combines-features), and both must be [in the same VPC] [within the same account] (elb-nlb-alb-target-same-vpc-same-account).
plan.table: How the target learns the client IP (columns: In front of the target | Client IP arrives as): Application Load Balancer | the X-Forwarded-For header: the ALB [stores the IP address of the client] (elb-alb-xff-holds-client-ip); Network Load Balancer, instance targets or UDP | the source address: [Otherwise, the default is enabled] (elb-nlb-client-ip-preservation-defaults); Network Load Balancer, IP targets with TCP or TLS | not by default: [The default is disabled] (elb-nlb-client-ip-preservation-defaults); use proxy protocol; AWS PrivateLink consumers | the [private IP addresses of the load balancer nodes], unless proxy protocol is on (elb-privatelink-source-ip-is-lb-nodes).
plan.why: Why do the addresses stay fixed? The addresses of one Network Load Balancer [must be completely controlled by you] or completely by Elastic Load Balancing, so the [addresses known to your clients do not change] (elb-nlb-faq-no-mix-eip-and-elb-ips).
plan.exam_signal: "partners allow-list fixed IP addresses", "Elastic IP" or "millions of requests per second with low latency" point to a Network Load Balancer ([extreme performance and static IP is needed], elb-choose-nlb-for-layer4-extreme-performance-static-ip); "offer the service to other VPCs through AWS PrivateLink" points to it too: an endpoint service needs a [Network Load Balancer or a Gateway Load Balancer] (elb-privatelink-needs-nlb-or-gwlb; chapter 11).
plan.body_extras: Optional, only if words remain: the TCP idle timeout is [350 seconds] by default, adjustable to [60-6000 seconds] (elb-nlb-tcp-idle-timeout-default-350-seconds); for UDP it is [120 seconds] and [This cannot be changed] (elb-nlb-udp-idle-timeout-fixed-120-seconds).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: choose a Network Load Balancer when clients need fixed addresses, or TCP and UDP at very high speed. The thing to watch is client IP preservation, which depends on the target type and the protocol.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team deletes a Network Load Balancer that used two Elastic IP addresses. Are the addresses gone, and do they still cost money? Answer: they [will return to your allocated pool] and [be available for future use] (elb-nlb-faq-eip-returned-on-delete); there is [a charge for all Elastic IP addresses], used or idle (ec2-eip-charged-in-use-and-idle), so release the ones you do not need.

sections.heading: A Gateway Load Balancer passes packets through appliances without changing them

plan.problem: Security requires that all traffic into and out of the VPC pass through a fleet of third-party firewall appliances. The fleet must scale and survive the loss of one appliance.
trace: **Steer with routes.** The application subnet's route table sends traffic to a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint [as the next hop in the route table]; the endpoint and the servers are [in different subnets] (elb-gwlb-endpoint-next-hop-route-table). The endpoint [is a VPC endpoint] (elb-gwlb-endpoints-across-vpcs).

**Listen for everything.** The Gateway Load Balancer [listens for all IP packets across all ports] (elb-gwlb-layer-3-all-ports); [You cannot specify a protocol or port] for its listener (elb-gwlb-listener-no-protocol-port).

**Wrap and send.** It picks an appliance with a [5-tuple flow hash algorithm] and sends the packets with the [GENEVE protocol on port 6081] (elb-gwlb-5-tuple-geneve-6081); it [does not change any part of the packet] (elb-gwlb-faq-layer3-gateway-layer4-bump-in-wire).

**Return.** The appliance inspects the packet and sends it back; [both directions of a flow] go to the same appliance (elb-gwlb-faq-default-flow-5-tuple-both-directions), and the traffic continues to its destination.
plan.table: When appliances fail (columns: Event | What the Gateway Load Balancer does): one appliance fails | it [removes it from the routing list] and [reroutes traffic to a healthy appliance instance] (elb-gwlb-faq-one-appliance-fails-reroute); flows that already exist, default setting | it keeps them on the old target: [send existing flows to the same target], while [new flows are sent to healthy targets] (elb-gwlb-target-failover-default-no-rebalance); every appliance in one zone fails | it [will drop the network traffic]; AWS recommends [deploying Gateway Load Balancers in multiple AZs] (elb-gwlb-faq-all-appliances-in-az-fail-drop).
plan.why: Why a separate type? The traffic is not addressed to the load balancer: a Gateway Load Balancer is for [deploying inline virtual appliances] and is [invisible to the source and destination] (elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances).
plan.exam_signal: "inspect all traffic with third-party firewall, intrusion detection or deep packet inspection appliances" points to a Gateway Load Balancer ([such as firewalls], elb-gwlb-virtual-appliances); "one central fleet of appliances for many VPCs or accounts" points to Gateway Load Balancer endpoints, because the appliances [can reside in different AWS accounts and VPCs] (elb-gwlb-faq-endpoint-centralize-appliances).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: a Gateway Load Balancer [does not perform TLS termination] and [does not maintain any application state] (elb-gwlb-faq-no-tls-termination-no-app-state); the appliances' security groups allow [inbound and outbound traffic on port 6081] (elb-gwlb-no-security-groups).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a Gateway Load Balancer puts your firewall appliances into the traffic path, and route tables send the traffic there. The thing to watch is that clients never address it; route table entries do.
plan.stop_and_answer: Users connect over FTP through the appliance fleet. The control connection and the data connection reach different appliances, and transfers break. Which setting helps? Answer: change flow stickiness from the default 5-tuple to [3-tuple (source IP, destination IP, IP protocol)] or [2-tuple (source IP, destination IP)] (elb-gwlb-faq-3-or-2-tuple-for-control-data-apps).

sections.heading: You pay for each load balancer hour and its busiest capacity dimension

plan.problem: A startup runs one load balancer for a test environment that gets almost no traffic, and one for production before a big launch. Both appear on the bill.
trace: **Hours.** An Application, Network or Gateway Load Balancer is charged for [each hour or partial hour] it runs, and a partial hour is [billed as a full hour] (elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour).
**Capacity units.** It also pays for the capacity units [used per minute] (elb-capacity-units-billed-per-minute).

**Busiest dimension.** For an ALB the dimensions are [new connections, active connections, bandwidth and rule evaluations], and the bill uses the [maximum resource consumed amongst the four dimensions] (elb-alb-faq-lcu-four-dimensions-max): [You are charged only on] the [dimension with the highest usage] (elb-lcu-charged-on-highest-dimension).
**Extras.** You also pay [standard AWS data transfer charges] and [standard public IPv4 address charges] (elb-pricing-public-ipv4-and-data-transfer-extra).
plan.table: What one ALB capacity unit includes (columns: Dimension | One LCU): new connections | [25 new connections per second] (elb-alb-lcu-25-new-connections-per-second); active connections | [3,000 active connections per minute] (elb-alb-lcu-3000-active-connections-per-minute); processed bytes | [1 GB per hour] for EC2 instances, containers and IP addresses (elb-alb-lcu-1-gb-per-hour-processed); rule evaluations | [1,000 rule evaluations per second]; the [first 10 processed rules are free] (elb-alb-lcu-first-10-rules-free).
plan.why: Why bill by the busiest dimension? Elastic Load Balancing [scales your load balancer capacity automatically] (elb-scales-capacity-automatically), so the bill follows the capacity that the traffic needs, not a size that you picked.
plan.exam_signal: "a sudden, very large spike at a known time, such as a launch event" points to an LCU reservation, which can [reserve a static minimum capacity] (elb-lcu-reservation-static-minimum-capacity); "cut cost for many small applications with their own load balancers" points to one ALB with host and path rules (elb-alb-host-conditions-many-domains-one-lb).
plan.body_extras: One sentence each, only if words remain: with a reservation you pay for capacity [reserved per minute] and for use [beyond your reserved LCUs] (elb-lcu-reservation-billing). Metrics arrive in [60-second intervals] while requests flow (elb-metrics-60-second-intervals); access logs are [disabled by default] and land in [stores them in the Amazon S3 bucket] (elb-access-logs-off-by-default-s3).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: you pay for every hour the load balancer exists, plus its busiest capacity dimension. The thing to watch is that an idle load balancer still pays the hourly charge.
plan.stop_and_answer: In one hour an ALB uses 4 LCUs of new connections, 10 LCUs of active connections, 2 LCUs of processed bytes and no rule evaluations beyond the free ones. How many LCUs are billed for that hour? Answer: 10; the bill uses the [maximum resource consumed amongst the four dimensions] (elb-alb-faq-lcu-four-dimensions-max). The prompt numbers are example values; the reveal sentence carries the fact link.

sections.heading: FAQ quick-fire
sections.plan: Ten 'FAQ <n>.' prompts (see faq), each answered in one clause in its reveal and followed by an AWS quote block of whole sentences from the fact's evidence quote. At most 450 words.

traps.belief: An Application Load Balancer has fixed IP addresses, or you can attach Elastic IP addresses to it, so partners can allow-list it.
traps.truth: In the AWS feature table only the Network Load Balancer has static or Elastic IP addresses. An ALB's DNS name resolves to node addresses that Elastic Load Balancing remaps as it scales (TTL of 60 seconds). For fixed addresses in front of ALB features, put a Network Load Balancer with an ALB-type target group in front, or use AWS Global Accelerator.

traps.belief: When an instance fails its health checks, the load balancer terminates it and launches a replacement.
traps.truth: The load balancer only stops routing to an unhealthy target and resumes when it is healthy again. EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the instance, and only when the Auto Scaling group uses ELB health checks; by default it ignores them.

traps.belief: A Network Load Balancer cannot have security groups, so the targets must allow the client addresses directly.
traps.truth: Since 2023-08-10 a Network Load Balancer can have security groups, but only when you create it; then the targets can allow only the load balancer's security group, and clients cannot reach them directly.

traps.belief: When every target fails its health checks, the load balancer stops sending requests to them.
traps.truth: When all targets fail their health checks at the same time in all enabled zones, the load balancer fails open and routes requests to all of them; a 503 comes when the target group has no registered targets.

traps.belief: An HTTPS listener with a certificate keeps the traffic encrypted all the way to the instances.
traps.truth: The HTTPS listener terminates TLS and decrypts at the load balancer. The hop to the targets is encrypted only with an HTTPS target group (the ALB re-encrypts) or with a Network Load Balancer TCP listener on port 443 that passes the encrypted traffic through.

traps.belief: Putting a load balancer in front of instances removes the single point of failure, even if all the instances run in one Availability Zone.
traps.truth: A load balancer serves the zones you enable, and targets in a zone that is not enabled get no traffic. Production in only one Availability Zone is an anti-pattern: run targets in two or more zones and enable a subnet in each (an ALB needs at least two).

traps.belief: Instances behind an internet-facing load balancer need public IP addresses in public subnets, so the load balancer can reach them.
traps.truth: Internet-facing and internal load balancers both route to targets by private IP address, so the targets need no public IP addresses and can sit in private subnets.

traps.belief: A Network Load Balancer can route requests by URL path or host name, like an Application Load Balancer, only faster.
traps.truth: A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and picks a target with a flow hash; host, path and header conditions are listener rules of the Application Load Balancer, which works at layer 7.

traps.belief: Each service or domain name needs its own load balancer.
traps.truth: One Application Load Balancer routes to many target groups with host and path conditions, and each load balancer is billed for every hour it runs, so several services usually share one ALB.

traps.belief: One HTTPS listener can present only one certificate, so each domain needs its own listener or load balancer.
traps.truth: An HTTPS listener has one default certificate plus a certificate list; with SNI it serves several domains on the same port with a different certificate for each, and an ALB holds 25 certificates by default besides the default one.

traps.belief: Sticky sessions are the way to keep user sessions safe in a scalable web tier.
traps.truth: Sticky sessions only send a user back to the same target; the session still lives on that one instance, and stickiness can unbalance the load. AWS calls a centralized session store the ideal solution when the web fleet is elastic.

traps.belief: Cross-zone load balancing is on, and free, for every type of load balancer.
traps.truth: On an Application Load Balancer cross-zone is on by default and has no regional data transfer charge. On Network and Gateway Load Balancers it is off by default, and turning it on adds charges for data transfer between Availability Zones.

traps.belief: To send all traffic through a fleet of third-party firewall appliances, put a Network Load Balancer in front of them.
traps.truth: Inline appliances, where the traffic is not addressed to the load balancer, need a Gateway Load Balancer: route tables send traffic to a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint, and the Gateway Load Balancer passes packets through the appliances without changing them.

question_slots.note: A company runs six small web applications in one AWS Region, each with its own domain name and its own Application Load Balancer; traffic is low. MOST cost-effective change. Key: one ALB with an HTTPS listener, a certificate for each domain in the certificate list, and host-header rules that forward to six target groups (elb-alb-host-conditions-many-domains-one-lb, elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains, elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour). Distractors: keep six ALBs, one per application, and lower their idle timeouts (trap elb-trap-one-lb-per-service); one Network Load Balancer with six listeners on different ports (trap elb-trap-nlb-routes-by-path is not exact: use misconception 'users would have to add port numbers'); keep six ALBs and turn off cross-zone load balancing to avoid data transfer charges (misconception: the ALB has no such charge, elb-alb-cross-zone-no-data-transfer-charge). No AWS sentence says one ALB is cheaper; the explanation derives it from the per-load-balancer hourly charge (brief.v0 d103).

Key: (A) an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule for path /api/* that forwards to a second target group (elb-alb-path-conditions-smaller-services). A team wants a new path of its existing ALB to run a Lambda function with no servers to manage; requests and responses are small JSON documents (state it, so that the 1 MB limit does not decide). Key: a target group of type lambda with the function registered, and a listener rule that forwards to it (elb-alb-target-types-instance-ip-lambda, lambda-trigger-alb-sync). Distractors: a Network Load Balancer target group of type lambda (impossible-feature; why links elb-lambda-target-alb-only); an EC2 instance that receives the request and invokes the function (violates-qualifier: a server to manage); a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the function (misconception).

An internet-facing Network Load Balancer has one subnet, in AZ 1, and all its EC2 targets run in AZ 1. The application must keep serving clients if an Availability Zone fails. Select TWO. Keys: enable a subnet in a second Availability Zone on the load balancer (elb-nlb-enable-disable-az-any-time, elb-node-per-enabled-az); run targets in that second zone, for example with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones (elb-targets-in-disabled-az-no-traffic as the why). A large customer now requires fixed IP addresses to allow-list; the path rules must stay; LEAST operational overhead; one Region, one VPC. Key: add the three certificates to the HTTPS listener's certificate list; SNI selects the certificate by hostname (elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains, elb-faq-sni-automatic-multiple-certificates). Distractors: three HTTPS listeners on ports 443, 8443 and 9443 (trap elb-trap-one-certificate-per-listener); three ALBs, one per website (trap elb-trap-one-lb-per-service); certificates on the instances behind a TCP Network Load Balancer (violates-qualifier: more certificates to manage).

Instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB sometimes hang: their EC2 status checks pass, the ALB marks them unhealthy, but they stay in service for days. Replace them automatically with the LEAST operational overhead. Key: turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group (ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on, ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default, ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace). Distractors: lower the ALB unhealthy threshold so that the load balancer replaces them sooner (trap elb-trap-lb-replaces-instance); a scheduled Lambda function that terminates instances the ALB reports as unhealthy (violates-qualifier: custom code); increase the deregistration delay (misconception).

After a release, the application answers the path / with a redirect to the sign-in page (HTTP 302). Every target in the ALB target group is now unhealthy, yet users can still use the site. Which change fixes the health checks? Key: point the health check at a path that returns 200, such as /health, or add 302 to the success codes, which can be [200 to 499] (elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200, elb-alb-health-check-path-default-slash). The explanation says why users can still reach the site: [the load balancer fails open] (elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy). Distractors: nothing to fix, because the load balancer already stopped sending requests to the unhealthy targets (trap elb-trap-all-unhealthy-stops-traffic); change the health check protocol to TCP (impossible-feature for an ALB: [the possible protocols are HTTP and HTTPS], elb-alb-health-check-protocol-default-http); raise the unhealthy threshold to its maximum (misconception: it delays but does not fix).

question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair C (twin q17)
question_slots.note: A web application keeps session data in instance memory; behind an ALB, users are signed out when a request reaches another instance. Changed phrase: 'The fix must be in place by tomorrow and must not need code changes.' Key: (A) turn on duration-based stickiness for the target group (elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what, elb-alb-sticky-duration-vs-application-cookie). Options identical in q17: (A) duration-based stickiness on the target group; (B) store sessions in Amazon ElastiCache, read by every instance (ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data, elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers; fails q13: code change); (C) replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer with source IP stickiness (misconception, elb-nlb-sticky-source-ip, elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat); (D) turn off cross-zone load balancing so that each user stays in one zone (misconception: stickiness is not supported with cross-zone off, elb-alb-sticky-not-with-cross-zone-off).

A three-tier application: the web tier receives traffic from the internet; the application tier must be reachable only from the web tier, and each tier scales on its own. Select TWO. Keys: an internet-facing ALB in public subnets that forwards to the web tier; an internal ALB that the web servers call and that forwards to the application tier (elb-multi-tier-internet-facing-plus-internal, elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only). Distractors: one internet-facing ALB with a path rule that forwards /app/* to the application tier (misconception: the application tier becomes reachable from the internet); application servers with public IP addresses registered with the internet-facing ALB (trap elb-trap-targets-need-public-ip); a Gateway Load Balancer between the tiers (trap elb-trap-nlb-for-inline-appliances does not fit; use misconception).

Users who type http:// must end up on HTTPS; an ALB already has an HTTPS listener. LEAST operational overhead. Key: an HTTP listener on port 80 whose default action redirects to HTTPS with HTTP 301 (elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https, elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb). Distractors: change the application code to return the redirect (works, but more effort: trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-works-means-correct); delete the port 80 listener (misconception: users who type http:// get an error); a fixed-response action that tells users to type https:// (misconception, elb-alb-fixed-response-action).

A Network Load Balancer with default settings has two targets in AZ 1 and six in AZ 2; the AZ 1 targets are overloaded while clients are spread evenly over both zones. LEAST operational overhead to spread the load evenly over all targets. Key: turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group or the load balancer, and accept the data transfer charge between zones (elb-nlb-gwlb-cross-zone-off-by-default, elb-nlb-cross-zone-lb-and-tg-level, elb-nlb-faq-cross-zone-regional-data-transfer-charged). Distractors: nothing to change, because cross-zone is already on for every load balancer (trap elb-trap-cross-zone-same-for-all); switch the target group to the least outstanding requests algorithm (misconception: an NLB selects targets [using a flow hash algorithm], elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection); turn on source IP stickiness (misconception, elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat).

Changed phrase: 'Users must keep their sessions when an instance is terminated during scale-in.' Key: (B) store sessions in Amazon ElastiCache (ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data, elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers). Same four options as q13; option A carries trap elb-trap-sticky-sessions-keep-state.

Uploads to instances behind an ALB take up to 10 minutes. During scale-in, some uploads fail. Key: raise the target group's deregistration delay above the longest upload; the default is [300 seconds] and the range [0 to 3600 seconds] (elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds, elb-alb-deregistration-waits-for-in-flight). Distractors: raise the load balancer idle timeout (misconception: it concerns idle connections, elb-alb-idle-timeout-default-60-seconds); turn on sticky sessions (misconception); lengthen the health check interval (misconception).

An ALB with cross-zone load balancing on serves targets in three zones. In one zone, responses become slow, but the targets still pass their health checks. Move traffic away from that zone as soon as possible with the LEAST operational overhead, and return it later. Key: start a zonal shift for the ALB in Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC), with zonal shift turned on for the load balancer (elb-zonal-shift-what, elb-alb-zonal-shift-off-by-default-one-az, elb-alb-zonal-shift-cross-zone-enabled). Distractors: wait for the health checks to remove the zone (misconception: the targets pass, so nothing changes); deregister that zone's targets one by one and register them again later (works, but more effort and slower: violates-qualifier); create a new ALB in the other two zones and change DNS (violates-qualifier).

An ALB's HTTPS listener uses a certificate from a third-party certificate authority that was imported into ACM. Last year it expired and the site was down. Prevent this with the LEAST operational overhead. Key: request a public certificate from ACM for the domain and replace the listener certificate; ACM renews it (elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically, acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal, acm-alb-renewal-in-flight). Distractors: rely on ACM managed renewal for the imported certificate (trap secrets-certificates-trap-acm-renews-everything); upload the certificate to IAM instead (misconception: you still renew it, acm-alb-certificate-from-acm-or-iam); install the certificate on the instances behind a TCP Network Load Balancer (violates-qualifier).

An internet-facing Network Load Balancer was created years ago without security groups; its instance targets allow TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 so that clients can reach them through it. Restrict the instances to traffic that comes through the load balancer, MOST secure. Key: create a new Network Load Balancer with a security group, allow port 443 on the targets only from that security group, and move clients to the new DNS name (elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation, elb-nlb-sg-reference-blocks-direct-access, elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg). Distractors: attach a security group to the existing load balancer (impossible-feature; why links elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation); keep 0.0.0.0/0, because a Network Load Balancer cannot have security groups (trap elb-trap-nlb-no-security-groups); allow only the load balancer's private IP addresses on the targets (misconception: with instance targets the client IP is preserved, elb-nlb-client-ip-preservation-defaults).

All traffic into and out of several VPCs must pass through a fleet of third-party firewall appliances in one central security VPC; the fleet must scale. Key: a Gateway Load Balancer in the security VPC, Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in each VPC, and route table entries that send traffic to the endpoints (elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances, elb-gwlb-faq-endpoint-centralize-appliances, elb-gwlb-endpoint-next-hop-route-table). Distractors: a Network Load Balancer in front of the appliances, with every client pointed at its DNS name (trap elb-trap-nlb-for-inline-appliances); an ALB with an AWS WAF web ACL (misconception: the requirement names third-party appliances and all traffic, not only web requests); VPC peering connections from each VPC to the security VPC (misconception: peering does not steer traffic through appliances).

tasks.title: Read the TLS policy and the load balancer quotas of your account
tasks.kills: "The certificate decides which TLS versions a client can use."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, read-only, 3 minutes, $0: read the security policy that the console gives a new HTTPS listener (aws elbv2 describe-ssl-policies --names ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-PQ-2025-09, query the SslProtocols): the expected output lists the TLS protocol versions, which come from the policy, not from the certificate (elb-alb-security-policy-protocols-ciphers, elb-alb-https-default-security-policy). Then read the same for ELBSecurityPolicy-2016-08, the default of the AWS CLI, and compare the protocol lists. Then aws elbv2 describe-account-limits (expect the application-load-balancers limit; the default is [50 Application Load Balancers], elb-alb-quota-load-balancers-per-region). Optionally list existing load balancers with their Type and Scheme (may be empty). Creates nothing. Commands from official CLI pages in the corpus (tasks check-cli --reference).

tasks.title: Route requests by path with listener rules, then break the rule order
tasks.kills: "The most specific rule wins, whatever its priority."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, in the default VPC, no instances, about one load balancer hour (cost line: the ALB is billed for [each hour or partial hour], elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour, plus public IPv4 address charges, elb-pricing-public-ipv4-and-data-transfer-extra; no prices). Read CloudShell's public address (curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com). Create a security group saa-elb-t02 tagged book=saa and task=elb-t02 that allows TCP 80 only from that address (no 0.0.0.0/0). Create an internet-facing ALB saa-elb-t02 in two default subnets of different zones (elb-alb-subnets-two-azs-different), tagged book=saa and task=elb-t02. Create an HTTP:80 listener whose default action is a fixed-response 404 (elb-alb-fixed-response-action). Add rule priority 20: path-pattern /api/* -> fixed-response 200 'api'. Wait until the load balancer is active (aws elbv2 wait load-balancer-available); curl /api/orders (expect 'api') and /other (expect 404 from the default rule, elb-alb-default-rule-last-no-conditions). Break it: predict, then add rule priority 10: path-pattern /* -> fixed-response 200 'catch-all'; curl /api/orders again: expect 'catch-all', because rules are checked [from the lowest value to the highest value] (elb-alb-rules-lowest-priority-first). Fix: set-rule-priorities to move the catch-all rule to priority 30; curl again: expect 'api'. Cleanup: delete-load-balancer (its listeners and rules go with it), wait load-balancers-deleted, delete-security-group. Verify: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=task,Values=elb-t02 returns nothing (T108). Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'.

tasks.title: Watch target health: an empty target group, then an unreachable target
tasks.kills: "When every target fails its health checks, the load balancer stops sending requests to them."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, in the default VPC, no instances, about one load balancer hour (same cost line as elb-t02). Create security group saa-elb-t03 (TCP 80 only from CloudShell's address) and an internet-facing ALB saa-elb-t03 in two default subnets, both tagged book=saa and task=elb-t03. Create target group saa-elb-t03 with target type ip and an HTTP health check (tagged the same), and an HTTP:80 listener that forwards to it. curl the load balancer: expect HTTP 503, because the target group has [have no registered targets] (elb-alb-503-no-registered-targets). Break it: predict, then register one private address that answers nothing, for example 10.255.255.10 with AvailabilityZone=all (RFC 1918 range for targets outside the VPC: elb-alb-faq-ip-target-ranges); describe-target-health shows initial, then unhealthy (elb-alb-target-state-initial, elb-alb-target-state-unhealthy). curl again: expect an HTTP 5XX error after a delay, not the fast 503, because with only unhealthy targets [the load balancer fails open] (elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy) and tries the target, which has a [connection timeout expired (10 seconds)] (elb-alb-target-connection-timeout-10-seconds). Fix: deregister the target; describe-target-health shows draining (elb-alb-target-state-draining), then the target is gone. Cleanup: delete-load-balancer, wait load-balancers-deleted, delete-target-group, delete-security-group. Verify by the tag task=elb-t03 (T108). Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'. speak.prompt: Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer: what decides it for a web application like ours?
speak.note: First sentence may start 'Both'. Short answer: for a web application that must route by URL path, an Application Load Balancer; a Network Load Balancer when you need fixed IP addresses, TCP or UDP, or extreme performance. How it works: the ALB reads each HTTP request and applies rules; the NLB reads connections and never sees the URL. Watch: if you need both, put a Network Load Balancer in front of the Application Load Balancer. In your case: 'Does any customer need to allow-list fixed IP addresses for our site?' Must not say: 'a Network Load Balancer can route by path'; 'you can attach an Elastic IP address to an Application Load Balancer'; 'a Network Load Balancer is always the better choice because it is faster'.

speak.persona: a fintech founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Our customer's firewall team wants fixed IP addresses for our API. We use an Application Load Balancer. What do we do?
speak.note: Short answer: keep the Application Load Balancer and put something with fixed addresses in front: a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses, or AWS Global Accelerator. How it works: the Application Load Balancer's addresses change as it scales, so you never hand them out; the Network Load Balancer forwards to the Application Load Balancer, which keeps your path rules. Watch: Global Accelerator also helps when you later run in more than one Region. In your case: 'Do your customers' firewalls need the addresses in one Region only, or worldwide?' Must not say: 'attach an Elastic IP address to the Application Load Balancer'; 'give them the current IP addresses; they do not change'.

speak.prompt: Our auditor says patient data must be encrypted all the way to the servers. Is HTTPS on the load balancer enough?
speak.note: Short answer: not by itself; the HTTPS listener decrypts at the load balancer, so you also need HTTPS from the load balancer to the servers. How it works: the load balancer ends TLS, reads the request and opens a second encrypted connection to each server; if the load balancer must never see the data, a Network Load Balancer passes the encrypted traffic through to the servers instead. Watch: the Application Load Balancer encrypts that second hop but does not check the server's certificate. In your case: 'Does the auditor accept that the load balancer sees the decrypted request for a moment?' Must not say: 'HTTPS on the load balancer encrypts everything to the servers'; 'the load balancer checks the server certificate'.

speak.prompt: If one AWS data center fails during the launch, will our customers notice?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain 'Availability Zone' as 'a separate group of data centers' the first time. Short answer: mostly not; the load balancer has an entry point in each of our three zones and sends users only to healthy servers. How it works: health checks find servers that stop answering, and the load balancer moves new requests to the servers in the other zones. Watch: a few requests can fail in the seconds before the health checks notice, and we pay for spare capacity in each zone. In your case: 'Can the other two zones carry the launch traffic on their own?' Must not say: 'nobody will notice anything'; 'the load balancer moves us to another Region'; 'the load balancer replaces the broken servers'.

diagrams.title: Callvale after: an Application Load Balancer in three zones
diagrams.claim: Users reach an Application Load Balancer with a node in three zones, and it sends requests to the healthy web instances in private subnets.
diagrams.alt: After: users connect over HTTPS to an Application Load Balancer in public subnets in AZ 1, AZ 2 and AZ 3. It forwards requests to one web instance in a private subnet in each zone. The instance in AZ 2 is marked unhealthy and gets no requests.
say: Users connect over HTTPS to the load balancer's DNS name.
The HTTPS listener ends TLS with an ACM certificate.
A node in each Availability Zone forwards requests to the target group.
Health checks find the failed instance, and it gets no new requests.
The instances accept traffic only from the load balancer's security group.
diagrams.note: At most 8 nodes: users, ALB (alb icon, across three public subnets or one ALB node with three zone groups), three web instances in private subnets (AZ 2 marked unhealthy), an ACM certificate label on the listener. No Auto Scaling group (chapter 17 comes next), no CloudFront, no Route 53 (chapters 15 and 13 come after), no WAF. No numbers in labels or steps. Step 5 holds 'only': link it to elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg (L705).
